The threespot chromis (Chromis verater) is a relatively large-bodied damselfish endemic to the Hawaiian Archipelago, where it inhabits deep coral reefs and rocky escarpments. Field surveys using stereo-video photogrammetry indicate that the species attains a maximum recorded standard length of 16 centimeters [Li = 16 centimeters], placing it among the larger members of the genus. This ultimate size is achieved through a protracted growth trajectory that spans several years, with individuals showing the most rapid elongation during the first two years of life before approaching an asymptotic plateau. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from demersal nest-guarded egg clutches at a remarkably small size; the wet weight at birth for this species has been estimated at approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with an egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, and the duration of this yolk-dependent period is brief. When incubated at a stable water temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C], the age at birth, defined as the timing of eclosion from the chorion, is approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days], after which the yolk-sac larva begins its transition toward exogenous feeding.

Sexual maturation in Chromis verater occurs at a body size considerably smaller than the species' ultimate length, a pattern common among iteroparous coral-reef fishes with indeterminate growth. Detailed gonadal histology from specimens collected across the main Hawaiian Islands reveals that the onset of gametogenesis, including the initial stages of vitellogenesis in females and spermatogenesis in males, is consistently associated with individuals reaching a standard length at puberty of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from length-weight regressions fitted to local population samples, is approximately 8.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 8.9 grams]. This transition to reproductive viability is marked by a distinct inflection in the allometric relationship between body length and mass, a shift that reflects the energetic demands of gonad development alongside continued somatic growth. The attainment of this pubertal threshold appears to be more strongly correlated with body size than with chronological age, though thermal conditions during early development likely modulate the growth rate necessary to reach this critical size.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized through both laboratory observations of captive pairs and in situ monitoring of nest-guarding males across a range of depths and sites. During the peak of the summer spawning season at water temperatures around 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C], individual females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate characterized by the production of roughly 200 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 200 eggs per day]. This rate is not sustained year-round; rather, it represents the upper bound of daily fecundity during optimal foraging and thermal conditions, and it closely matches the maximum reproductive output reported for the congeneric Chromis chromis from Mediterranean populations. The daily egg production requires significant energetic investment, and gravid females typically show reduced feeding activity immediately prior to spawning. Males establish and defend nesting territories on rocky substrata, cleaning a nest site to which females are then courted. Following external fertilization, the male assumes sole responsibility for egg guarding and fanning, behaviors that are critical for ensuring adequate oxygen delivery to the developing embryos.

As individuals continue to grow and accumulate somatic tissue beyond the onset of reproduction, they gradually approach their physiological maximum size. The ultimate wet weight for Chromis verater, based on the length-weight relationship estimated from a large sample of adults across the species' range, is approximately 71 grams [Wwi = approximately 71 grams]. This asymptotic mass, achieved at the largest recorded standard length of 16 centimeters, represents the point at which somatic growth effectively ceases due to the energetic constraints of maintenance, reproduction, and the physical limitations of the body cavity. Reaching this size requires several years of sustained feeding on zooplankton and benthic invertebrates, and individuals in the oldest age classes are characterized by heavier, thicker bones and more developed musculature compared to younger conspecifics. Despite the cessation of further elongation, these large adults continue to reproduce actively throughout their remaining lifespan, contributing disproportionately to the next generation's recruitment due to their higher fecundity and competitive advantage in nest-site defense.

Long-term mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation have provided robust data on the longevity of this species. The maximum documented lifespan for the threespot chromis maintained under natural reef conditions at an ambient water temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C] is approximately 5110 days [am = approximately 5110 days], equivalent to roughly 14 years. This extended lifespan is notable among Hawaiian reef fishes and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by slow growth, delayed senescence, and high adult survival rates. The combination of a relatively long lifespan with high annual fecundity, in which each female may produce thousands of eggs per year, results in a substantial lifetime reproductive output that buffers the population against the high and variable mortality experienced during the planktonic larval phase. Such demographic resilience is likely a key factor enabling Chromis verater to maintain stable populations despite the substantial predation pressure exerted by piscivorous fishes, particularly at the settlement and early juvenile stages when individuals are most vulnerable.
